evidence.title: Investigating How Clinicians Form Trust in an AI-Based Mental Health Model: Qualitative Case Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported trust formation with uncertainty visualization in an AI mental health screening model
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported that violin-plot visualization of confidence and uncertainty supported trust and aligned with their expectations of decision ambiguity. Qualitative only, with no numeric effect.
evidence.quote: Trust formation was supported by the explainability of the model, particularly through (1) visualization of confidence and uncertainty through violin plots, aligning with the clinicians' expectations of decision ambiguity; (2) feature attribution for and against predictions, which mirrored clinical reasoning; and (3) use of pseudo-sumscores in the AI model, which increased interpretability by presenting explanations in familiar clinical formats.

evidence.title: Not All Uncertainty Is Equal: How Uncertainty Granularity Shapes Human Verification in LLM-Assisted Decision Making
evidence.outcome: Effect of displayed uncertainty at different granularities on user reliance and verification
evidence.effect: Relation-level uncertainty reduced external verification (internet searches, checking URLs), steering users toward reliance on the LLM and its uncertainty cues; token-level increased agreement.
evidence.quote: Notably, relation-level uncertainty also reduced external verification (i.e., internet searches, checking provided URLs), steering users away from independent fact-checking and toward reliance on the LLM and its accompanying uncertainty cues.

evidence.title: Calibrating trust in AI-assisted pituitary surgery
evidence.outcome: Clinician trust calibration and performance with confidence labels on AI outlines
evidence.effect: When AI performed worst, trust was lower in Enhanced group (3.00 vs 3.67, p=.035), sustained in final clip (3.67 vs 4.33, p=.019). Less dispersion in Enhanced when AI inaccurate (IQR 0.07 vs 0.21, p=.004).
evidence.quote: However, when AI performed worst, trust was significantly lower for the Enhanced group (3.00 vs 3.67, U=668, p=.035), sustained in the final clip (3.67 vs 4.33 U=687, p=.019).

evidence.title: Novel Entropy-Based Framework for Quantifying Dynamic Epistemic Uncertainty in Clinical Medicine
evidence.outcome: Whether entropy-based uncertainty visualization tracks LLM diagnostic reasoning uncertainty across rounds in pilot cases
evidence.effect: Unconfounded cerebellar infarction case showed monotonic entropy decay from 2.15 to 1.74; ambiguous pneumothorax case had sustained high entropy (~2.41); acute cholangitis showed top-1 rank stagnation. Pilot only, three cases, no clinician outcomes.
evidence.quote: Pilot validation across representative emergency medicine scenarios demonstrated distinct topological and information-theoretic behaviors: unconfounded cases (cerebellar infarction) exhibited smooth geodesic progression toward the ground truth alongside monotonic Shannon entropy decay from 2.15 to 1.74; noisy environments with ambiguous findings (spontaneous pneumothorax) suffered from trajectory wandering, local minimum traps, and high sustained entropy (~2.41) due to insufficient repulsive weighting for negative evidence; and triage-conflicted cases (acute cholangitis) achieved precise geometric proximity to the true node but experienced top-1 rank stagnation because the model conflated acute severity triage (sepsis) with anatomical etiology.

evidence.title: Determinants of Reader-LLM Interaction in Thoracic Radiology: Impact of Model Confidence and Reader Expertise
evidence.outcome: Association of model confidence with readers' adequate acceptance or rejection of LLM suggestions
evidence.effect: Model confidence associated with adequate interaction (OR 3.82, 95% CI 1.58-9.25), with weaker effect among experts (OR 0.79).

commentary.bottom_line: Offline studies suggest patient-level uncertainty estimates can separate likely errors from reliable predictions, and one simulated trial found that confidence labels lowered clinician trust when the AI performed poorly. No study has tested displaying these estimates in live care with patient outcomes, and one trial found that uncertainty cues reduced users' independent verification.

perspectives.view: Of 17 studies, two simulated randomized trials measured how people respond to displayed uncertainty, and their findings differ. Confidence labels lowered clinician trust when the AI performed worst (3.00 vs 3.67, p=.035). Relation-level uncertainty reduced users' external verification. The remaining studies are mostly offline benchmarks of the estimates themselves, which gives only indirect support for the display practice.

Conformal flagging at 90% confidence reduced errors from 34.6% to 10.5% internally and from 43.8% to 11.8% externally, which suggests flags may route likely errors to review. One segmentation model was overconfident. In fundus imaging, estimated uncertainty correlated weakly with clinician assessments (r 0.156–0.548). Uncertainty cues may also reduce independent checking.

In a Danish deployment, clinicians said violin-plot uncertainty displays matched their sense of case ambiguity, although the study measured no effect. Display format appears to matter, since token-level and relation-level displays shifted reliance differently. In a segmentation triage study, an uncertainty threshold auto-accepted 60% of cases at 96% negative predictive value, which may reduce review burden.

One Scottish study of older adults found a high-confidence subgroup of about 35% of scans with accuracy near 80%, compared with 66.8% across all scans. In another study, entropy flagged 90.7% of out-of-distribution predictions as uncertain. This may matter where local patients differ from the training data, but no study tested that directly.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to describe the statistical confidence of predictions. FUTURE-AI calls for calibrated per-patient estimates. The FDA text concerns disclosure in marketing submissions and does not require a per-output display to clinicians. No supplied study tests whether such labeling changes clinical decisions.

Flagging creates review work. At 90% confidence, 29.4% of cases internally and 38.6% externally were flagged for clinician review. Confidence thresholding in another study kept 46% of samples for high-confidence prediction. Abstention in a pancreatic tumor study reached 19.5% in one margin band. Health systems would need to plan staffing for flagged cases before adoption.

In a Korean reader study, higher model confidence was associated with readers correctly accepting or rejecting LLM suggestions (OR 3.82, 95% CI 1.58-9.25), and the effect was weaker among experts. This suggests confidence displays may help less experienced clinicians decide when to override the AI. No study measured patient outcomes or asked patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested per-output uncertainty displays in live clinical workflows with patient outcomes, error rates, or override behavior as endpoints. Prospective comparative studies should measure whether displays improve clinician decisions and whether clinicians still verify outputs independently. They should also track how calibration holds after deployment and what review workload the flags create.
commentary.underserved_note: No study testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One study included older adults in Scotland. The available evidence therefore cannot show whether uncertainty estimates stay calibrated for these patients. It also cannot show whether confidence displays help or mislead clinicians caring for them.
